title: (Say nothing)
why:
I've already been on stage, so the short version: Kaspar, Head of Umbraco at Kraftvaerk, MVP, I sit on the CMS Advisory Board, and I make packages. Some of them are even useful.
This is a slightly different talk for me. Usually I show up with “look at this crazy thing I've built”, or “here's how to break Umbraco to get your way”. Not today. Today I'm here to share some knowledge. Knowledge that I've dug out with my own dirty hands and knowledge that was known once, and lost.
It started almost two years ago as a pun. The 10 UmbraCommandments. What if I wrote down guiding principles for how we build Umbraco, and made them sound like they came in the form of gospel? I'm a huge believer that if you can find a fun angle on something, almost anything becomes enjoyable. Even guiding principles.
Strong opinions, held loosely. I don't expect you to agree with all of it, and I'd love to be argued with.
disclaimer:
Quick disclaimer. I'm not a religious person myself, but it's still important for me to say: I am not here to bash anyone's religion or faith. I'm using the idea of ten commandments as a vehicle for a fun take on best practice. The only religion we make fun of here is the definitely-not-a-cult religion of Umbraco, so elegantly launched at Codegarden last year.
(read the last line: “And also definitely not cursed.” Let it hang. Don't react to anything.)
revelation:
So. You won't believe this, but it definitely happened. I went up Mount Bellissima. A shining U in the sky showered me in a blue light, and there they were. Two tablets.
And a voice said: “Take these tablets, and go forth, and spread the gospel.” So here I am.
But here's the thing. They weren't new. They were old. Ancient. Dusty. Like someone had carried them up there a long time ago and everyone just… forgot to go and look. Knowledge older than any of us, or like - older than someone who is 10.
And by complete coincidence, it completly matches my personal preference for how we should build our Umbraco sites.
[PRESS] [CUT OK: this press] (the camera zooms into the tablets until the tiny text is readable; once it lands, the right-hand tablet rewrites itself)
(let the room read both. Say nothing, or: “Worth it.”)
tablets:
[NEW · ~5 s]
Ten umbracommandments. 
(don't read them out. Let them look, then click into the first one.)
c1:
Number one. 
Content is not composable.

We've been here before. This was my first ever meetup talk, I built BlockFilter as a workaround, and I bring it up whenever I can. Today is no exception.
Compositions are a contract written in blood. You put a block list on a "grid compostion", editors fill it with content, and one day someone removes that composition from the document type. Every single piece of data associated with that composition is now gone. Not hidden. Gone. Not even revisions can save you.
So for "content-crucial" things - share the data type, never the composition. Compose the safe things: settings, meta, call to actions, references.
The guiding question: would there still be a page left worth visiting if you removed the composition? And if not, could you at least derive a fallback from what's left?
c1-demo:
Here, to the left is a document type, Article [PRESS], with a composition called Content Blocks. 
That composition gives it a Body [PRESS] which is a block list. 
And here to the right [PRESS], a page, full of blocks.
Lets swap the data-type of Body.
[PRESS] 
Datatype swap is ok. Assuming the underlying configuration is the same or close enough. Every block is still there.
Now lets swap the composition with something that -also- has the body datatype.
[PRESS] 
[PRESS] (Yes. Article Blocks goes in and the Body comes back: same alias, same data type. The blocks crumble anyway.)
Composition swap is a deletion. Even when the new composition is identical.
(Point at the history.) [PRESS] And no, the history won't save you. Not one of those versions remembers the Body - and that is why the first Umbracommandment is "Content is not composable"
c2:
The second Umbracommandment

There are four content types.

There aren't really four. Umbraco gives you a document type and an element type and of you go. But unless document types get categories, we'll talk our way out of it. So lets do that.
[PRESS]Page: it renders, and you can compose onto it. 
[PRESS]Block: it renders, but only inside a list, a grid (or a rich text editor if you are into that kind of thing), and you never use it as a composition.
[PRESS]Data: an element that never renders on its own, block settings, menu items, accordion items in an accordion block.
[PRESS]Composition: it exists only to be composed. Never picked, never rendered.
Each of them gets a root folder in the document types in settings. After that, I don't care.
This means any developer in any project that adheres to this umbracommandment will always know where to start looking.
Now. The eagle-eyed among you…
[PRESS] (zoom onto the tablet: it still says six, and “seven is right out”)
…will notice the tablet says six. There used to be six and there still are in umbraco 17 or older.
[PRESS] (the chisel strikes: six becomes four, seven becomes five)
Stone is really hard to edit.
[PRESS] (back out to the whole card)
Repository and Repository Item. [PRESS]With Umbraco 18's Library, shared content lives as Library elements now. They have ascended. We do not mourn them. We count to four. Unless you are on Umbraco 17 or lower, then we count to 6.
c2-types:
[NEW · ~5 s]
Can we just agree that it is hillarious that this is a real umbraco backoffice embedded directly in my presentation?

It's running the Clean starter kit, which while SUPER useful, is also super useful for this presentation as it breaks at least 6 or 7 of the 10 umbracommandments.

It sorta agrees there are 4 content types, we just don't agree on their names or categorization. We will get back to that later.
[PRESS] (a spotlight on its document type folders)
c3:
Three. The root is bare, and a folder is only a folder.

So what can go in folders? Well, data types, content types, media and dictionary items.

[PRESS]Your data type folder is a window into how much you respect the next developer.
I already think it's unfortunate that Umbraco dumps every data type in the root, including the ones it auto-creates from the content type creation flow. Things could be so nice. 
Data types you create should live in Custom or BrandName, in a folder named after the editor alias. Use good names. Reuse before you create a new one.
[PRESS]Media is the first part of a solution to spiral out of control, so give it the best starting chance: nothing at the media root. 
[PRESS]Document types go in their type folders per the second umbracommandment.
And a folder is only a folder. 
[PRESS]If a dictionary item holds a value, it isn't a folder anymore.
Folders are free. Regret is not.

And I'm not the only one. Lotte, four years ago: your heart sinks.

c4:
The 4th Umbracommandment.

Compose in your IComposer, not in Program.cs - or elsewhere.

This one is hopefully non-controversial. Program.cs uses the minimal hosting model. Let's keep it minimal.
Program.cs is what starts the whole bloody thing. It wires everything together. It should be a masterpiece. IComposers are ordered, discoverable and dependency-aware. A bloated Program.cs just means nobody agreed where things go.
Things that aren't Umbraco's, App Insights, CORS, go into extension methods on the WebApplicationBuilder.
One composer or many? I go back and forth between one all-mighty composer and one per feature. I lean towards one all-mighty composer per project, but I'd love to hear other perspectives.
Huh, that's weird, the CORS looks a little funky there. Anyway.

[NEW · ~20 s]
We've all seen these kinds of messes.
[PRESS] (the card turns over)
c4-clean:
[NEW · ~10 s]
Lets try to keep it as close to the default as we can.
c5:
Umbracommandment number 5
A production site runs in production mode.

If your editors can edit templates in production, you don't have a CMS. You have a loaded gun.
I see this all the time. 
Umbraco has runtime modes: use Production in production. Set the application URL, build with configuration release, HTTPS only, no models builder generating things, no template editing.

Now I would love it, if Umbracos production mode also prevented schema-changes - but as it stands, an admin can easily completly destroy a site by editing content types. You can stop them by making a little notificationhandler that just denies that, based of the - you guessed it - runtime mode.

If you have a dedicated frontend server but still use MVC, remove the backoffice entirely from that server by editing a couple of lines in program.cs
(optional, small) Did that word just… no. Moving on.
c6:
Six. Thy names. Aliases are code. Code is English. End of discussion.
Even if you call your document type “Artikel side”, do everyone a favour and make its alias articlePage. Danish belongs in labels, not in your strongly-typed models. I don't want to read Artikel.Where.NogetPaaDansk. Neither do you. Neither does the next developer, who might not be Danish.
(optional, one beat, at the zalgo'd word) Hm.
[PRESS]camelCase for aliases. articleHeadline, not ArticleHeadline. 
[PRESS]Translation keys: PascalCase, dot-separated. Site.Navigation.Home. Consistent keys can be fed into other systems.
c6-dict:
(live) The dictionary. Umbraco doesn't really have folders in here. Translations apparently aren't a top priority, which is also why you can't get them out through the Delivery API. But items can have children, and that's folder-like enough. Remember III: the parent holds no value.
[PRESS] (a spotlight on the keys, none with a parent)
[PRESS] (the card turns over)
c6-dict-after:
[NEW · ~5 s]
Grouped by their keys. ContactForm, and under it ContactForm dot Email, Message, Name, Send. Boring. Beautiful.
c7:
[NEW · ~45 s]
I… What the heck is happening to my text?!
(read the title) Views render. They don't search.
Your view should know where the fruit is, not climb every branch to find it.
Everyone has a Descendants in a navigation partial somewhere. Model dot Root dot Descendants of something, then a Where clause. 

It's fine with fifty pages. Then the site suddenly has ten thousand.
Don't over-query either: the same traversal in five partials is five traversals. 
No IContentService in a view: the cache is for reading, services are for writing. And if you really must search, search something that was built for searching.
c7-code: This one. You've written it. I've written it.

Every page view. Every node. To find five menu items.

[PRESS] (zoom to the opener)

c8:
[NEW · ~35 s]
Ok, these slides are definitely getting darker…
(read the title) 
8th Umbracommandment
Umbraco is not your database.
The content tree is for content. Not your form submissions, not your order log, not your nightly import of forty thousand products.
If it changes every minute, it isn't content. If an editor will never open it, it isn't content. Bulk imports go into custom tables.
Your data doesn't belong in the tree. And as we'll see in a moment, your settings don't belong only in the database either.

[PRESS] (the column scrolls)

Back to the scripture.

Same page. When you need to store data that changes a lot, use a custom database table or another service. It's been there all along.
c9:
[REVISED · ~75 s]
I'm starting to feel a little cold… It's definitely gotten a lot darker… We soldier on!
(read the title) A root node is not a rendering node.
I used to say a root node could only be a Repository. Repositories ascended, remember? So the tablet needs fixing.
[PRESS] (zoom onto the tablet: the chisel carves the new line)
The root is a template-less shell, and the pages live beneath it. One site: www, and home under it. Many sites: site-a slash home, site-b slash home.
[PRESS]
This is the one we can fight over. Take the Clean starter kit and imagine it going multi-site, with a second Home start node. What's cleaner: a Home root that isn't called Home, despite having the title Home, or a root that contains it? And that root can hold the settings and other bits and pieces.
Permissions get easy too. A Home-rooted site sprawls into Home, Settings, Shared Content, Events… With a bare root, you grant an editor one node per site. Done.
And guess what. This isn't new either.

Thanks for pointing this out Sebastiaan - It was december 2010 - and I can only assume Sebastiaan is feeling very old now - anyway, he wrote about "The Ultimate Site Structure setup"

[PRESS] (zoom to its warning banner)
(It's been so long it even has a nice warning on the site these days)

[PRESS] (zoom to the structure)
Two nodes: Site settings, and Home. A root that doesn't render, with Home beneath it. Commandment nine. Sixteen years early.

[PRESS] (down to the comments)
The last comment, November 2012, reads: “This is exactly what I used to do… up until today.”
c9-root:
[NEW · ~10 s]
(live) And here's the content root of our demo site running the clean starter kit. [PRESS] (a spotlight on Home) Home rendering right there at the root. Sinful.
c10:
[REVISED · ~65 s]
…I am just gonna ignore that.
It is a sin not to usync 
when not on Umbraco Cloud

The last one, and I want to push it further than I used to.
uSync all the things. Unless you're on Umbraco Cloud, then Umbraco Deploy all the things. Don't do both at once. I've tried, it's a bad time.
But here's the hard part: if the solution needs it to work, it travels with the repository. Including the settings you invented. If your package or your dashboard keeps its settings in a custom table, it owes you a uSync handler, or a JSON file on disk. You built a feature. You didn't build its migration path.
And the uncomfortable part, back to nine: that Site Settings node is content. Content doesn't travel with git. Editor-facing settings go in a node. Developer settings, keys, flags, endpoints, go in config. Either way, in source control. No exceptions.

After the fix the next press goes back to the very same page: the same property, now the type's own, nothing inherited. (Spotlight, then back to the board.)
3. II and III · auto-sort: document types, data types and media into their folders.
4. IV · the Program.cs cleanse: a web request rewrites Program.cs and edits the csproj. On stage. On purpose.

recap:
So - we've made it. Lets summarize.
Content is not composable. Four content types. The root is bare, and a folder is only a folder. Compose in your composer. Production runs in production mode. English camelCase aliases, PascalCase keys. Views render, they don't search. Umbraco is not your database. The root does not render. And uSync, unless you're on Cloud.
These are the Umbracommandments - and we are all sinners.
bonus:
[REVISED · ~15 s]
And one more. The bonus commandment.
Do whatever is right for your project and remember to have fun, I'm not your mum.
Strong opinions, held loosely. Come and argue with me.
